request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 69-year-old male with a known duodenal diverticulum and remote history of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery, was admitted to the hospital with bilateral upper quadrant abdominal pain for several weeks, nausea, abdominal distension, and food intolerance. A CT scan revealed a distended gastric remnant and a possible bowel obstruction.

The patient was taken to the operating room for an exploratory laparotomy where a 4.5 cm enterolith was found and removed from the distal jejunum. A cholecystectomy was also performed during which gallstones were discovered. The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged on postoperative day 8.

Follow-up:
At the patient's postoperative visit, two weeks after surgery, he was reported to be in good health. Unfortunately, the patient was lost to follow-up after one month.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Summary:
This 69-year-old male presented with bilateral upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea, abdominal distension, and food intolerance. He was found to have a distended gastric remnant and a bowel obstruction caused by a 4.5 cm enterolith containing bile salts. Treatment included an exploratory laparotomy and enterolith removal, as well as a cholecystectomy. The patient had an uneventful recovery and was discharged on postoperative day 8. It is unfortunate that the patient was lost to follow-up after one month.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
**CODE: K56**

The principal diagnosis is the bowel obstruction caused by the jejunal enterolith. The obstruction is the condition that was treated and that led to admission. The enterolith is its cause, and the cholecystectomy and gallstones are secondary findings. The obstruction falls under chapter K (digestive system), category K56 (paralytic ileus and intestinal obstruction without hernia).
